ety.text: From Middle English ambre, aumbre, from Old French aumbre, ambre, from Arabic عَنْبَر (ʕanbar, “ambergris”), from Middle Persian 𐭠𐭭𐭡𐭫 (ʾnbl /⁠ambar⁠/, “ambergris”). Compare English lamber, ambergris. Displaced Middle English smulting (from Old English smelting (“amber”)), Old English eolhsand (“amber”), Old English glær (“amber”), and Old English sāp (“amber, resin, pomade”).

senses.d: Ambergris, the waxy product of the sperm whale.
ex: Slaves […] with silver Censors […] perfum'd the air with Amber, Aloes wood, and other Scents.
Ambre is hote and drye […] Some say that it is the sparme of a whale.

senses.d: Formerly thought to be the product of a plant.

A hard, generally yellow to brown translucent or transparent fossil resin from extinct coniferous trees of the pine genus, used for jewellery, decoration and later dissolved as a binder in varnishes. One variety, blue amber, appears blue rather than yellow under direct sunlight.
ex:
With scarfs and fans and double change of bravery,
With amber bracelets, beads, and all this knavery.

senses.d: A yellow-orange colour.
The intermediate light in a set of three traffic lights, which when illuminated indicates that drivers should stop when safe to do so. See also yellow light.
ex: While earlier controllers provided concurrent ambers, present practice is to indicate a minimum intergreen period of 4 s.
Also flashing ambers are not operational at this type of crossing.

senses.d: The stop codon (nucleotide triplet) "UAG", or a mutant which has this stop codon at a premature place in its DNA sequence.
ex: an amber codon, an amber mutation, an amber suppressor

senses.d: Hesitance to proceed, or limited approval to proceed; an amber light.
ex: […] in response to the actions I just described, business was given the green light, and now we seem to be on amber.

senses.d: Of a brownish yellow colour, like that of most amber.
ex: Ahead, a cool breeze swept the pale morning sun across a grassy meadow turned amber by morning's frost.

senses.d: To perfume or flavour with ambergris.
ex: ambered wine, an ambered room

senses.d: To preserve in amber.
ex: an ambered fly

senses.d: To cause to take on the yellow colour of amber.
ex: For purple mountains majesty; for amber waves of grain.
The firelight flickered on her rounded cheeks, ambering the pale skin.

senses.d: To take on the yellow colour of amber.

senses.d: An official messenger and representative.
A corporate representative, often the public face of the company.
ex: As front hall porter, you are an ambassador for the hotel.

senses.d: A player who is an excellent role-model and who upholds the integrity of the game and thereby contributes to the sport's popularity and growth.

senses.d: An object of an ardent desire.
ex: My ambition is to own a helicopter.

senses.d: A desire, as in (sense 1), for another person to achieve these things.
A personal quality similar to motivation, not necessarily tied to a single goal.
The act of going about to solicit or obtain an office, or any other object of desire; canvassing.
ex: I on th' other ſide / Us'd no ambition to commend my deeds, […]

senses.d: To seek after ambitiously or eagerly; to covet.

From Middle English enbuschen, from Old French enbuscier, anbuchier (verb) (whence Middle French embusche (noun)), from Old French en- + Vulgar Latin boscus (“wood”) (whence also bouquet), from Frankish *busk (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush, heavy stick”). Compare ambuscade. The change to am- from earlier forms in en- is unexplained. More at bush.

senses.d: The act of concealing oneself and lying in wait to attack or kill by surprise.
An attack launched from a concealed position.
ex: Heaven, whose high walls fear no assault or siege / Or ambush from the deep.

senses.d: The concealed position or state from which a surprise attack is launched.
ex:
the Georgean hills,
Whoſe tops are couered with Tartarian theeues,
That lie in ambuſh, waiting for a pray:

senses.d: The troops posted in a concealed place, for attacking by surprise; those who lie in wait.
A group of tigers.
ex: He outwits a positive ambush of tigers who want to eat him up and take his beautiful new clothes

senses.d: To station in ambush with a view to surprise an enemy.
ex: By ambuſh’d men, behind their Temple laid, / VVe have the King of Mexico betray’d.

senses.d: To attack by ambush; to waylay.

The atmosphere; the surrounding air or sky; atmospheric components collectively such as air, clouds, water vapour, hail, etc.
